title: The Grid and the Mask: Textile, Dance, and the Rooms She Built
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Davos to Munich: An Education in Materials

stops.name: Davos-Platz, born in the sanatorium valley
stops.date_confidence: attested; German and English Wikipedia agree on 19 January 1889 at Davos-Platz
stops.campa: Sophie Henriette Gertrud Taeuber is born in Davos-Platz, in a valley whose entire economy is lungs: sanatoria stacked up the slope, invalids from every capital in Europe wheeled out onto balconies for the thin dry air. Her father Emil Taeuber, Prussian by birth, keeps the pharmacy that supplies them. She is the youngest of five. Two years later tuberculosis takes him. He is the man who sold the valley its remedies. Her mother reacquires the Swiss citizenship she had given up by marrying a foreigner.
suggested_refs: The Taeuber pharmacy at Davos-Platz, in the sanatorium town of the 1880s

stops.name: Trogen, the pension her mother builds
stops.date_confidence: attested for the family's resettlement in Trogen and for the mother running a guesthouse there (German Wikipedia; English Wikipedia). The house name Pension Taeuber and an opening around 1902 come from the dossier lead alone and are [R]. Month and day defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The widow moves her children across Switzerland to Trogen in Appenzell Ausserrhoden and there does a thing that will be repeated: she designs a building and then lives inside it. The guesthouse takes paying visitors and the daughters help run it. Sophie grows up in a house that is also a business, where curtains, linen, dishes and the arrangement of a room are neither decoration nor art but the working surface of the day. She learns to draw here, and to embroider, and no one in the household ranks one above the other. She is six when they arrive.
suggested_refs: The guesthouse at Trogen designed and run by Sophie Taeuber's mother

stops.name: Vevey, a year of boarding school above the lake
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout: the Mesdames van Muyden school at Vevey and the year 1905-06 come from the dossier lead only and were not located on any independently accessible source in this pass. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: For a single year she is sent west into French-speaking Switzerland, to a girls' boarding school on the terraces above Lake Geneva. Most short accounts of her life leave the episode out entirely. What it gives her, if the record is right, is French: the language she will later live in at Strasbourg and Clamart, take citizenship in, and edit a trilingual journal in. The school's own archive has not been reached. The whole year rests on one uncorroborated line in a chronology.
suggested_refs: The Mesdames van Muyden boarding school at Vevey, unlocated
sources: Dossier lead; no independent source located

stops.name: St. Gallen, the textile department
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1906-1910 in the textile department of the Ecole des arts decoratifs, St. Gallen, under Johannes Stauffacher (1850-1916), a school founded 11 November 1867 by the chamber of commerce and industry of St. Gallen-Appenzell (German Wikipedia). The dossier's naming of the institution as the Industrie- und Gewerbemuseum is an error and is corrected here. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: St. Gallen lives on embroidery. Its machines supply lace collars to half the world, and its school of decorative arts, founded by the chamber of commerce, exists to feed those machines with drawings. Under Johannes Stauffacher she spends four years learning how a motif is disciplined: reduced, squared, made to repeat, made to survive being woven ten thousand times. It is a training in constraint before it is a training in beauty. The grid she will paint in 1915 is already in the loom she is learning to draw for.
suggested_refs: The Ecole des arts decoratifs, St. Gallen, textile department, and the teaching of Johannes Stauffacher

stops.name: Munich, the Debschitz School
stops.date_confidence: attested that she entered the Lehr- und Versuch-Ateliers fuer angewandte und freie Kunst of Wilhelm von Debschitz and Hermann Obrist in 1910 and graduated in 1914 (German Wikipedia). English Wikipedia compresses the attendance to 1911 and 1913; the precise October 1910 start is the dossier's reconstruction and is [R]
stops.campa: Wilhelm von Debschitz and Hermann Obrist run their teaching and experimental studios on a principle that is heresy in most academies: no hierarchy between the crafts and the fine arts. A student weaves, makes lace, turns wood, draws a building, and none of it ranks above the rest. Taeuber takes all of it. She is twenty-one, and she will hold the position for the rest of her life without once arguing for it. The question of whether her cushion covers count as art gets asked by other people.
suggested_refs: The Debschitz School, Munich, and Hermann Obrist's reform-craft pedagogy

stops.name: Hamburg, a year at the loom
stops.date_confidence: attested for a year of weaving study at the Kunstgewerbeschule Hamburg in 1912-13 (German and English Wikipedia). Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: She interrupts Munich for a year at the Hamburg school of arts and crafts to study weaving. Hamburg is flat and commercial, a North Sea port with no mountain anywhere in it, and she is there alone at twenty-three. The instruction is arithmetic before it is design: warp and weft, the count of threads, a pattern that must close on itself or fail on the frame. She comes back to Bavaria holding two trades, neither of them painting. Weaving admits no gesture and no correction. The thread goes where the count sends it, and a mistake is not painted over but unpicked.
suggested_refs: The weaving workshop of the Kunstgewerbeschule Hamburg, 1912-13

stops.name: Munich, the teaching diploma
stops.date_confidence: attested that she completed the Debschitz School in summer 1914 with a qualification to teach (German Wikipedia); the month of June is the dossier's precision and is [R]
stops.campa: She finishes the Debschitz course with a diploma that licenses her to teach, which in 1914 is the only reliable route by which a woman with her training will draw a salary. She is twenty-five. Nothing she has made so far would strike anyone as radical: textile designs, exercises in lace and turned wood, competent and largely anonymous work in the reform-craft manner of the school. Six weeks after she takes the diploma, Austria sends its ultimatum to Serbia.
suggested_refs: The Debschitz School teaching diploma, summer 1914

segments.name: Zurich, 1914-1915: Movement and the Right Angle

stops.name: Zurich, moving in with Erika
stops.date_confidence: attested that she returned to neutral Switzerland in 1914 after the diploma and moved in with her sister Erika Schlegel in Zurich (German Wikipedia). The precise month, November, is dossier-only and is [R]
stops.campa: War closes Germany to her and she crosses into neutral Switzerland, to Zurich, where her sister Erika Schlegel keeps a household. Erika will matter more than any patron: she reads, she writes, she believes in what her younger sister is doing before anyone else does, and twenty-eight years later, when Sophie is going hungry in the unoccupied zone of France, it is Erika who posts the food parcels. For now the city is filling up with refugees, deserters, pacifists and draft-dodging poets out of four belligerent countries, all of them talking.
suggested_refs: Erika Taeuber Schlegel's Zurich household, refuge of 1914 and of 1942

stops.name: Zurich, the Laban school of movement
stops.date_confidence: attested that she trained in Bewegungskunst under Rudolf von Laban in Zurich from 1915 and joined the Schweizerischer Werkbund the same year (German and English Wikipedia). 'From summer 1915' and the July date are ordering devices and are [R]. Building coordinate not pinned; central Zurich used
stops.campa: Rudolf von Laban has moved his school of movement art to Zurich for the duration, and Sophie Taeuber enrolls in it. His assistant Mary Wigman runs much of the teaching, Suzanne Perrottet plays for the classes, and Katja Wulff trains beside her. Laban is not making dances so much as building a notation for space, a way of writing down where a body is and how it got there. Textile, movement and drawing have become one problem to her, and she stops keeping them apart. She joins the Schweizerischer Werkbund the same year.
suggested_refs: Laban's wartime Zurich school and the beginnings of movement notation

stops.name: Zurich, the first vertical-horizontal compositions
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1915 (German Wikipedia). No month or day is recorded, so this stop is defaulted to 01-01 and precedes the Laban enrollment in this file only by that convention; the two are concurrent
stops.campa: In colored pencil on paper she sets down rectangles in rows: no figure, no horizon, no reference to anything outside the sheet. She is twenty-six, unknown, teaching nowhere yet, exhibiting nowhere, and she makes them in a rented Zurich room in a country at peace surrounded by countries that are not. Arp, who has not yet met her, will spend the next three decades telling people that these sheets came before his own work and changed it. They are among the earliest fully abstract works made by anyone in Europe.
stops.quote: The clear tranquillity of Sophie Taeuber's vertical and horizontal compositions influenced the diagonal, baroque dynamics of my abstract creations.
stops.quote_source: Hans (Jean) Arp, quoted in Tate Etc, issue 52 (Summer 2021)
suggested_refs: The 1915 vertical-horizontal compositions in colored pencil
sources: Tate Etc, issue 52 (Summer 2021), 'Sophie Taeuber-Arp: colour, geometry and pure radiance'

stops.name: Galerie Tanner, Zurich: meeting Hans Arp
stops.date_confidence: attested that they met at a Zurich exhibition in November 1915, commonly identified as the Galerie Tanner (English Wikipedia). The gallery's exact 1915 street address was not located, so the coordinate is central Zurich and approximate; the day is defaulted
stops.campa: At an exhibition of modern work she meets Hans Arp, a Strasbourg poet and collagist who has come to Switzerland to stay out of a German uniform and is telling consulates, as required, that he is a citizen of whichever country is not currently conscripting him. They begin working together almost at once, cutting and pasting papers, making objects neither of them will afterwards be able to divide into his and hers. The Zurich circle calls them the Arps long before there is a marriage. She goes on signing her own work Taeuber.
suggested_refs: The Galerie Tanner, Zurich, and the joint duo-collages of 1916-18

segments.name: Dada: The Mask, the Marionette, the Salary

stops.name: Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse 1: the cellar
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Cabaret Voltaire's opening on 5 February 1916 under Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings, and for Taeuber's association with the circle (German Wikipedia). No dated print establishes that any surviving photograph of her masked and costumed was taken in this room; the popular Cabaret Voltaire caption is flagged in the scholarship and is not asserted here. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from laban.journey.json, suzanne_perrottet.journey.json and katja_wulff.journey.json
stops.campa: Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings open a cabaret in a narrow room off the Spiegelgasse, and within weeks it is producing simultaneous poems, Marcel Janco's painted cardboard masks and organized noise. The Laban dancers come down from the studio to it: Suzanne Perrottet at the piano with Schoenberg and Satie, Katja Wulff, Sophie Taeuber. She is by day a candidate for a municipal teaching post and by night behind a mask, and she does not mention the second in her application for the first. Which surviving photograph belongs to which evening in this room has never been settled.
suggested_refs: Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse 1
Marcel Janco's painted cardboard masks
Nell Andrew's archival study of the Dada dance photographs

stops.name: Kunstgewerbeschule Zuerich, the textile class
stops.date_confidence: attested that she took charge of the textile design class at the Zurich Kunstgewerbeschule in May 1916 and held it until 1929 (German and English Wikipedia). The exact day, 5 May, is dossier-only and is [R]. Building coordinate not pinned; central Zurich used
stops.campa: The city's school of arts and crafts gives her the textile design class, and she will hold it for thirteen years. It is the household's only reliable income, since Arp sells almost nothing through the whole Zurich period. She teaches embroidery, weaving and the construction of patterns to young women who will mostly go into the trade, and she teaches it as she was taught at St. Gallen and Munich, without conceding that the work ranks below a canvas. She holds the post until 1929, when she resigns it in order to leave the country.
stops.quote: Her lessons were all about strange materials and impractical stuff.
stops.quote_source: Elsi Giauque, a former student, quoted in Tate Etc, issue 52 (Summer 2021)
suggested_refs: Taeuber-Arp's teaching materials and pattern exercises, Kunstgewerbeschule Zurich, 1916-1929

stops.name: Galerie Dada, near the Paradeplatz: the abstract solos
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Galerie Dada's opening on 29 March 1917 in the former Galerie Corray premises, and for Taeuber dancing there to Hugo Ball's phonetic poems in a shamanic mask (German and English Wikipedia, which also credit Emmy Hennings with founding the gallery). Two corrections to the dossier: the mask is by Marcel Janco, not by Arp, and the coordinate is moved south from Bahnhofstrasse 19 to the Paradeplatz end of the street, since the dossier's 47.3757/8.5402 sits by the Hauptbahnhof, some 450 to 500 m too far north. German Wikipedia records only two documented solo Dada appearances by her in total
stops.campa: The gallery opens in the Bahnhofstrasse rooms Hans Corray had held, down by the Paradeplatz, and Emmy Hennings is credited with founding it. Taeuber dances alone to Hugo Ball's sound poems in one of Marcel Janco's shamanic masks, her face and body wholly hidden inside it. Ball watches from the side and writes down what he sees. She is at this moment a salaried instructor of the municipal school of arts and crafts, which is why the mask is not only an aesthetic decision. By the surviving record she gives exactly two documented solos of this kind.
stops.quote: A poetic sequence of sounds was enough to make each of the individual word particles produce the strangest visible effect on the hundred-jointed body of the dancer.
stops.quote_source: Hugo Ball, quoted in Tate Etc, issue 52 (Summer 2021)
suggested_refs: The Galerie Dada, former Galerie Corray, Bahnhofstrasse at the Paradeplatz
Marcel Janco's shamanic mask
Hugo Ball's Zurich diaries

stops.name: Monte Verita, Ascona: the Sun Festival
stops.date_confidence: attested that she took part in Laban's Sonnenfest at Monte Verita in 1917 alongside Mary Wigman, Suzanne Perrottet and Katja Wulff (English Wikipedia; dossier citing the Arp foundations). The August dating is corroborated only loosely and the exact festival date should be treated with caution; the day is defaulted
stops.campa: Laban brings his school south for the summer, up the hill above Ascona, where vegetarians, anarchists, theosophists and nudists have been running a colony since before the century turned. There is no proscenium and no ticket. The Sun Festival is danced outdoors in the open by a company that includes Mary Wigman, Suzanne Perrottet and Katja Wulff. Taeuber has spent the winter dancing in a cellar behind a mask. This week she dances on a hillside in full light, and it is the same training.
suggested_refs: Laban's Sonnenfest at Monte Verita, August 1917

stops.name: Zurich, the turned wooden heads
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1918 (German Wikipedia). Her membership of the group Das Neue Leben with Marcel Janco and Arp, exhibiting through 1920, is corroborated mainly through the dossier's cited foundations rather than a page fetched directly, and is [R]. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: On a lathe she turns a series of wooden heads and paints them: ovals on turned stands, the features reduced to a circle, a curve, a band of color, one of them titled as a portrait of Arp. They are hat-stand forms and they are also sculpture. A milliner's block and a portrait bust are here the same object, and she has never treated that as a contradiction to be resolved. She is also showing this year with Das Neue Leben, alongside Marcel Janco and Arp; the group goes on exhibiting until 1920.
suggested_refs: The painted Dada Heads of 1918-20, including the Arp portrait

stops.name: Zurich, the marionettes for Koenig Hirsch
stops.date_confidence: attested: Alfred Altherr, director of both the Zurich Kunstgewerbeschule and the Kunstgewerbemuseum, commissioned the marionettes, props and sets for Carlo Gozzi's Koenig Hirsch in Rene Morax's modern adaptation; premiere 11 September 1918 in Zurich, ignored by the Zurich press, with no second performance until 1965 in St. Gallen (German Wikipedia). The dossier omitted both Altherr and Morax
stops.campa: Alfred Altherr, who directs both the school where she teaches and the museum next door to it, commissions her to build a puppet theatre for the Werkbund exhibition: marionettes, props and sets for Carlo Gozzi's King Stag in Rene Morax's modern adaptation. She makes the figures out of turned wood and painted cylinders, jointed so that the joints show. The premiere is on the eleventh of September. The Zurich press ignores it entirely, and the production is not staged a second time until 1965, in St. Gallen.
suggested_refs: The Koenig Hirsch marionettes, Museum Bellerive and Kunstgewerbemuseum Zurich collections

stops.name: Pura, Ticino: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested for 20 October 1922 at Pura, Ticino (German Wikipedia). Coordinate corrected: the dossier's 45.9847/8.9236 falls near Bioggio, about four kilometres east across the valley; English Wikipedia places Pura at 45.9833/8.8667. No church or registry address located
stops.campa: After seven years they marry, in a village above Lake Lugano, on the twentieth of October, and she becomes Sophie Taeuber-Arp on paper. The hyphen is the only concession made. She goes on signing work Taeuber, keeps her salary, keeps her class in Zurich, and keeps making objects that neither of them signs at all because neither of them could afterwards say who did which part. For the next twenty years the sculptures are attributed to him and the textiles to her.
suggested_refs: The marriage register of Pura, Ticino, 20 October 1922

stops.name: Ruegen, the Baltic summer
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout: the 1923 holiday on Ruegen with Kurt Schwitters and Hannah Hoech comes from the dossier lead alone and was not confirmed against any accessible source. Island-centre coordinate; month and day arbitrary
stops.campa: The Arps take a Baltic holiday with Kurt Schwitters and Hannah Hoech, on an island of chalk cliffs and beech forest a long way north of anywhere either couple lives. Schwitters is building Merz out of tram tickets. Hoech is cutting the photographic record of the Weimar Republic into pieces. Zurich Dada is shaking hands with Hanover and Berlin on a beach. Nothing is known to have been produced there, and the whole episode rests on a single unconfirmed line.
suggested_refs: Correspondence between the Arps, Schwitters and Hoech, 1922-24
sources: Dossier lead; no independent source located

stops.name: Paris, the Swiss section of the 1925 Exposition
stops.date_confidence: attested that she was a member of the Swiss division of the Exposition internationale des arts decoratifs et industriels modernes in Paris, 1925 (Fondazione Marguerite Arp chronology). Two dossier claims are demoted to [R] and are not asserted as fact: that she received a prize, whose class no source names, and that Johannes Itten was her co-representative. German Wikipedia does not mention 1925 at all. Coordinate marks the Invalides site; her pavilion is not pinned. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Switzerland sends tapestries to the Paris exposition that will give the decorative arts of the decade their name, and Sophie Taeuber-Arp is in the Swiss section. She is thirty-six, and this is the first time Paris registers her, as a maker of textiles, in the city she will spend her last fourteen years in. The tradition adds two things the sources do not carry: a prize, whose class nobody can name, and Johannes Itten standing beside her as co-representative. Neither survives checking. Whether either was ever more than a chronicler's tidying, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The Swiss section of the 1925 Exposition internationale des arts decoratifs et industriels modernes
sources: Fondazione Marguerite Arp chronology, via dossier
itten.journey.json (relation asserted in the dossier, unconfirmed in that file)

stops.name: Strasbourg, French citizenship and the first interiors
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Arps established themselves at Strasbourg in 1926 and acquired French citizenship, and that she received interior commissions there (German Wikipedia; English Wikipedia on the residency requirement). The naming of the developers Andre and Paul Horn is dossier-only and is [R]. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Arp was born in Strasbourg when it was German. The city is French again, and residence there converts them both into French citizens. It also produces clients. She is commuting between Zurich, where she still teaches, and Alsace, where she is building, and she keeps that up for three years. Developers put her to work on apartments and hotels, and for the first time she is designing whole rooms rather than objects to be set inside somebody else's: walls, glass, floors, the color of a ceiling.
suggested_refs: The Horn apartment, Strasbourg, and the Alsatian interior commissions of 1926-28

stops.name: Strasbourg, the Hotel Hannong
stops.date_confidence: attested as her first large project, the wall design of the Hotel Hannong (German Wikipedia: 'Ihr erstes grosses Projekt war die Wandgestaltung des Hotel Hannong'), which upgrades the dossier's [R] on the commission itself. The further claim that the mural was later destroyed by fire is unverified and stays [R]. Hotel coordinate approximate to central Strasbourg; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Her first large architectural commission is the wall treatment of the Hotel Hannong: murals and stained glass for the entrance and the restaurant, geometry taken off the page and laid onto plaster at the scale of a public room. It is her first work at the size of a building, and she has never trained as an architect. Nobody eating there is looking at art. They are looking at the room they are eating in. The tradition says a fire took the mural. No source reached confirms it, and what became of the work is not established.
suggested_refs: The Hotel Hannong, Strasbourg, murals and stained glass, 1926-27

stops.name: Strasbourg, the stairwell at the Villa Heimendinger
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout: the villa, its stairwell mural of stylized dancing figures, and the detail that its owner was an ear-nose-throat specialist treating her come from the dossier lead alone and were not located on any accessible source. Coordinate is a central-Strasbourg placeholder, the villa's address being unknown. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: A doctor treating her for a throat complaint has her paint his stairwell, and she puts stylized dancing figures on it, the one place in the mature work where the body she trained under Laban comes back as a subject. Everything here is thin, and it is kept as a claim and not as a fact. Not even the year is firm: 1927 places the job among the other Alsatian commissions and does no more than that. The villa has not been located, the mural has not been photographed in anything reached, and the doctor arrives in the record without a first name.
suggested_refs: The Villa Heimendinger stairwell mural, Strasbourg, unlocated
sources: Dossier lead; no independent source located

stops.name: The Aubette, Place Kleber: the largest commission
stops.date_confidence: attested: renovation from 1926 to 1928, opening 16 February 1928, Place Kleber (French Wikipedia, 'Aubette (Strasbourg)'). One genuine attribution dispute is flagged and not resolved: the dossier gives Taeuber-Arp the Five O'Clock tea room, the bar, the billiard room and the entrance, while English Wikipedia assigns her the entrance hall, tea room and two bars, gives Arp the basement, passage and billiard room, and makes the stairwell a three-way collaboration
stops.campa: She is approached first, and she brings in the others: Arp, and then Theo van Doesburg out of De Stijl. Between them they turn an eighteenth-century building on the Place Kleber into a complex of bars, a cinema, a ballroom and a tea room, with every surface a composition. It opens in February 1928. Strasbourg does not like it. Within ten years the operator has papered most of it over, and by the time anyone is calling the place a Sistine Chapel of abstract art the rooms being praised have been under wallpaper for a generation.
stops.quote: The walls, covered with paintings, give the illusion of almost endlessly vast rooms.
stops.quote_source: Emmy Hennings on the Aubette interiors, quoted in Tate Etc, issue 52 (Summer 2021)
suggested_refs: The Aubette, Place Kleber, Strasbourg: 1938 overpainting, monument protection 1985 and 1989, restoration completed 2006

stops.name: Arosa, the cure
stops.date_confidence: attested that a lung illness sent her to Arosa during the Aubette years, exhausted by commuting between Zurich, Paris and Strasbourg, and that she spent the stay with Gala and Paul Eluard (German Wikipedia). This inverts the dossier, which staged an unattested c.1919-20 sanatorium stay as a stop and reduced the attested late-1920s one to a parenthesis; no source reached supports a 1919-20 stay. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Three years of trains between Zurich, Strasbourg and Paris put her lungs out. She goes up to Arosa in the Graubuenden, forty kilometres over the mountains from the Davos where her father died of tuberculosis and where the same industry of altitude and rest cures is still running. Gala and Paul Eluard are taking the same air that season. The largest commission of her working life has just opened in Strasbourg. She spends the months after it lying down.
suggested_refs: The Arosa cure stay with Gala and Paul Eluard, late 1920s

stops.name: Clamart, the house at the edge of the Meudon woods
stops.date_confidence: attested: a house constructed in 1927-28 at the edge of the Meudon forest to her design, occupied permanently from 1929 when she resigned the Zurich post (French Wikipedia, 'Fondation Arp', which supplies the coordinate 48.8036/2.2444; German Wikipedia). The street address, 21 rue des Chataigniers, comes from the dossier lead. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: With the Strasbourg money they buy land where the suburb runs out into the forest, and she draws the house: white, rectilinear, inexpensive, with separate studios on separate levels so that two people can work all day without seeing each other. It goes up through 1927 and 1928, and they move in for good in 1929. She is forty, and she has designed the building she will do her best work in without ever having been an architect. She resigns the Zurich class she has held since 1916 and gives up the salary with it. From here on there is no reliable income in the household at all.
suggested_refs: The Arp house and studios at Clamart-Meudon, now the Fondation Arp

stops.name: Paris, Cercle et Carre
stops.date_confidence: attested that she exhibited with Cercle et Carre in Paris in 1930 (dossier citing foundation biographical material; her general 1930s Paris activity is corroborated by English and German Wikipedia). Michel Seuphor's invitation is dossier-only and is [R]. Canonical Paris pin used; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Michel Seuphor and Joaquin Torres-Garcia gather the abstractionists of Paris into a group called Circle and Square, and she exhibits with them. Paris in 1930 is full of such groups, formed and dissolved over cafe tables by people who agree about geometry and about very little else, and she joins without ever writing a manifesto or signing a quarrel. Her name appears in the catalogues and not in the polemics. She had arrived at abstraction fifteen years before the group existed, alone, in a rented room. It lasts about a year.
suggested_refs: Cercle et Carre, Paris, 1930: the group's single exhibition and review

stops.name: Lodz, the museum the artists built
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Muzeum Sztuki opened to the public on 15 February 1931 as the International Collection of Modern Art assembled by the a.r. group, whose members included Wladyslaw Strzeminski, Katarzyna Kobro and Henryk Stazewski, the first museum of its kind in Europe (English Wikipedia). This corrects the dossier's '1931-32'. Her own contribution of work and her travel to the opening are dossier-only and remain [R]. City-centre coordinate
stops.campa: In an industrial city in Poland a handful of artists assemble a collection of international modern art by writing to everyone they admire and asking for a work, and a municipality agrees to house it. It opens in February 1931, the first museum of its kind in Europe, built by artists rather than by a state or a fortune. Wladyslaw Strzeminski, Katarzyna Kobro and Henryk Stazewski are behind it. Whether Sophie Taeuber-Arp sent work, and whether she travelled east to see it hung, the reachable record does not say.
suggested_refs: The International Collection of Modern Art, Muzeum Sztuki, Lodz, opened 15 February 1931
sources: Dossier lead for her participation, unconfirmed

stops.name: Paris, Abstraction-Creation
stops.date_confidence: attested that she was an active member of Abstraction-Creation in Paris in the 1930s, exhibiting and designing catalogues and invitations (German Wikipedia, which dates only to the decade). The dossier's tighter 1931-34 range is not independently confirmed by any source fetched. Canonical Paris pin; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The successor group is larger and better organized: hundreds of members across Europe, an annual publication, and a rule that the work be non-figurative. She had learned at St. Gallen that a motif is drawn to be reproduced and not to be admired, and nothing since has made her sort that labor below any other. She exhibits with the group, and she also lays out its catalogues and its invitation cards, the typography and the spacing, work that goes out under the group's name and not her own.
suggested_refs: Abstraction-Creation, Art non figuratif: the annual cahiers and Taeuber-Arp's layouts

stops.name: Kunsthalle Basel, twenty-four works
stops.date_confidence: attested: the 1937 group exhibition Konstruktivisten at the Kunsthalle Basel showed twenty-four works by Sophie Taeuber-Arp (German Wikipedia's exhibition list), which removes the dossier's hedge. Two further dossier claims are held apart: the 1932 Basel show at which more than ten of her wooden sculptures were allegedly exhibited under Arp's name alone is unverified and is [R]; and Allianz, which she joined in 1937, was founded by Richard Paul Lohse and Leo Leuppi, not by Max Bill, whom the dossier miscredits, and its own first group show was in 1938. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Basel hangs a survey of constructivist work and gives her twenty-four pieces in it, the largest showing of her own work under her own name that she will live to see. The same year she joins Allianz, the association of modern Swiss artists founded by Richard Paul Lohse and Leo Leuppi, in which Max Bill is a member and not, as the tradition has it, a founder. There is a counter-story attached to this building too: that a 1932 exhibition here showed ten of her turned-wood sculptures as Arp's. No source reached confirms it.
suggested_refs: Konstruktivisten, Kunsthalle Basel, 1937, catalogue and checklist

stops.name: Paris, the journal Plastique
stops.date_confidence: attested: plastique/PLASTIC was founded in 1937 by Albert Eugene Gallatin, the Paris-based Dutch artist Cesar Domela, George L. K. Morris and Sophie Taeuber-Arp, who acted as editor; trilingual in French, English and German, published in Paris and New York, five issues to 1939 (German Wikipedia). The dossier omitted Domela. Canonical Paris pin used although the journal was made between two cities; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: She edits a magazine. It is trilingual, French, English and German, printed in Paris and distributed from New York, funded by two American collectors, A. E. Gallatin and George L. K. Morris, with Cesar Domela as the fourth founder. She does the layout as well as the editing. Its subject is abstract art in a decade when abstract art is being taken down off museum walls in Germany and sold abroad as degenerate. Five issues appear. The last is dated 1939.
suggested_refs: plastique / PLASTIC, five issues, Paris and New York, 1937-1939

stops.name: Nerac, the road out
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Fondazione Marguerite Arp chronology records that in 1940 she fled to Grasse via Nerac and Veyrier ahead of the German entry into Paris in June, which upgrades the dossier's [R] on Nerac itself. The further claim that they were hosted at Nerac by Gabrielle Buffet-Picabia is unverified in every source reached and stays [R]. Day defaulted
stops.campa: They close the suitcases at Clamart and go south-west ahead of the German advance, leaving both studios and everything in them. Arp is abandoning fifteen years of sculpture without knowing when or how any of it will be seen again, and she reports him inconsolable. She writes from the middle of the departure to Annie and Oskar Mueller-Widmann, the Basel patrons who have been quietly buying her work for years. Nerac is a small town on the Baise in Lot-et-Garonne. They are there because somebody found them a room.
stops.quote: Your letter arrived just as I was closing our suitcases to leave. We've decided quite suddenly to go because a friend found us a room
stops.quote_source: Sophie Taeuber-Arp to Annie and Oskar Mueller-Widmann, June 1940, quoted in Hyperallergic, 'The Patrons Who Sustained Sophie Taeuber-Arp'
suggested_refs: The Mueller-Widmann correspondence, 1932-1942, Fondazione Marguerite Arp
sources: Hyperallergic, 'The Patrons Who Sustained Sophie Taeuber-Arp'

stops.name: Veyrier-du-Lac, the second stage
stops.date_confidence: attested that Veyrier lay on the 1940 route to Grasse (Fondazione Marguerite Arp) and that Peggy Guggenheim gave the Arps temporary shelter that year (German Wikipedia); the joining of the two, Guggenheim's household at Veyrier, is [R]. Coordinate corrected: the dossier's 46.1667/6.2167 is Veyrier in the canton of Geneva, in Switzerland, which they did not reach until late 1942; Veyrier-du-Lac in Haute-Savoie lies at 45.8822/6.1781, some 32 km south. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The route bends east to a lakeside village under the Alps. Peggy Guggenheim, who is at this moment getting a collection out of France by whatever means will carry it, shelters them for a time. The dossier puts that shelter here; the chronologies name the place and the person separately and never join them. They are both in their fifties, French by paperwork and stateless by circumstance, moving from address to address across a collapsing country with what they can carry. Where they sleep at Veyrier is not written down.
suggested_refs: Peggy Guggenheim's 1940 evacuation of her collection from France

stops.name: Grasse, the perfume town
stops.date_confidence: attested that they reached Grasse in 1940 and stayed until the flight to Switzerland, in poverty and malnutrition, with food parcels from Erika Schlegel and Marguerite Hagenbach, and with Sonia Delaunay-Terk as her working companion (German Wikipedia; Fondazione Marguerite Arp). The 'Chateau Folie' named by the dossier is unattested in every source reached and is [R]; Alberto Magnelli's presence in the circle is plausible but uncited here. Coordinate corrected from the dossier's 43.6667/6.9167. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: They stop in the hills behind Cannes, in a town that makes perfume and, in 1940, not much else. A small colony of refugee abstractionists forms around them. Sonia Delaunay comes, widowed in October 1941, and works alongside her. There is very little money. There is not always enough food, and parcels arrive from Erika Schlegel in Zurich and from Marguerite Hagenbach in Basel. The house the tradition calls the Chateau Folie appears in no source reached. Where in Grasse the two of them actually lived is not established.
stops.quote: We lived between a well, a graveyard, an echo and a bell.
stops.quote_source: Hans (Jean) Arp, recalling wartime Grasse, quoted in Tate Etc, issue 52 (Summer 2021)
suggested_refs: The Grasse refugee circle, 1940-42: Sonia Delaunay-Terk, the Arps, the food parcels from Zurich and Basel

stops.name: Grasse, the line drawings
stops.date_confidence: attested that she worked chiefly in pencil and colored pencil at Grasse in 1940-42, given wartime scarcity of paint and canvas, producing the geometric line-drawing series (German Wikipedia). The letter quoted is dated January 1942 and is placed at this stop for continuity. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Paint and canvas cannot be got in the unoccupied zone, so she works in pencil and colored pencil on paper, and the work changes under the constraint. The rectangles loosen into lines that curve and cross, wandering and geometric at the same moment, the series known as lignes geometriques et ondoyantes. It is the last invention of her life and it comes out of a shortage of materials. She is fifty-two. Between the drawings, by her own account, most of her day goes on finding something to eat.
stops.quote: most of my time is taken up with procuring food, which is becoming increasingly difficult
stops.quote_source: Sophie Taeuber-Arp to Annie and Oskar Mueller-Widmann, January 1942, quoted in Hyperallergic, 'The Patrons Who Sustained Sophie Taeuber-Arp'
suggested_refs: Lignes geometriques et ondoyantes and the Grasse drawings, 1941-42
sources: Hyperallergic, 'The Patrons Who Sustained Sophie Taeuber-Arp'

stops.name: Zurich, back across the border
stops.date_confidence: attested that they fled to Switzerland at the end of 1942, before the Germans reached Grasse, and that she spent her last New Year, 1942/43, at Max Bill's house in Zurich-Hoengg (German and English Wikipedia). The precise November dating and the household split, Sophie at Erika's and Arp at the Bills', are dossier-only and are [R]; that split also sits awkwardly with her death at the Bills' two months later. The dossier's claim that Johannes Itten welcomed her at an exhibition opening is likewise [R] and is not confirmed in itten.journey.json
stops.campa: German forces move into the southern zone and the Arps get over the border into Switzerland, twenty-eight years after she first crossed it in the other direction as a student running from a different war. She has no money and no studio. The tradition has her lodging with Erika while Arp lodges with Max and Binia Bill, and has Johannes Itten, a colleague from the same Swiss applied-arts world, greeting her at an exhibition opening. Neither detail is confirmed anywhere reached. She spends the New Year at the Bills' house in Hoengg.
suggested_refs: The Arps' crossing into Switzerland, late 1942

stops.name: New York, thirty-one women
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Exhibition by 31 Women opened at Peggy Guggenheim's Art of This Century on 5 January 1943, Taeuber-Arp is among the thirty-one, and English Wikipedia states she died a week after it opened. This corrects the dossier, which called her inclusion posthumous. Coordinate from the English Wikipedia article on the exhibition, replacing the dossier's value some 200 m off. She was not herself in New York
stops.campa: Peggy Guggenheim opens a show of thirty-one women artists on Fifty-Seventh Street on the fifth of January, and Sophie Taeuber-Arp is one of the thirty-one. She is in Zurich, penniless, and never sees it. It is the largest survey she is included in during her lifetime, and it hangs on another continent while she has nowhere of her own to work. The dossier had the exhibition down as posthumous. It is not: she is alive for the first nine days of its run.
suggested_refs: Exhibition by 31 Women, Art of This Century, New York, opened 5 January 1943

stops.name: Zurich-Hoengg, the garden house
stops.date_confidence: The death is attested; the calendar date is genuinely disputed and is not resolved here. German Wikipedia: she died in the night of 13 to 14 January 1943 of carbon monoxide poisoning from a badly handled stove in the Bills' garden house. English Wikipedia's infobox gives 14 January. The Fondazione Marguerite Arp gives the night of 13-14. Kunstmuseum Basel gives 13 January. The 12-13 January variant asserted in the dossier was found in no source at all. 14 January is the majority reading and is used; the minority reading of 13 January stands unresolved beside it
stops.campa: She spends the evening at Max and Binia Bill's house in Hoengg, on the edge of Zurich, and stays the night in the garden house on the property rather than cross the city again. The stove is handled wrongly. Carbon monoxide fills the small room and she does not wake. She has been back in Switzerland about two months, with no studio of her own. Her last drawings are on paper, made in a French hill town because there was nothing else there to work on. She is fifty-four.
suggested_refs: The garden house on Max and Binia Bill's property, Zurich-Hoengg
sources: Kunstmuseum Basel, 'Sophie Taeuber-Arp: Living Abstraction' retrospective page

stops.name: Locarno, the shared grave
stops.date_confidence: attested that Sophie Taeuber-Arp, Jean Arp and Marguerite Arp-Hagenbach share one grave in the Locarno cemetery, in successive burials of 1943, 1966 and 1994 (Fondazione Marguerite Arp, Marguerite Hagenbach page). That page names no cemetery and describes no monument. The plot is dated here to the first of the three burials; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: She is buried at Locarno, in the Italian-speaking canton. Arp lives another twenty-three years and marries Marguerite Hagenbach, who had been Sophie's own friend and one of the patrons posting food parcels to Grasse. For decades afterwards the estate presents the two artists as a single indivisible practice, which is the arrangement that makes her half of it hard to see. Arp is buried in the same plot in 1966. Hagenbach joins them in 1994. Three people in one grave.
suggested_refs: The Arp family grave, Locarno cemetery

stops.name: Kassel, documenta 1
stops.date_confidence: attested: documenta 1 ran at the Museum Fridericianum, Kassel, from 16 July to 18 September 1955 (English Wikipedia, 'documenta'), and Sophie Taeuber-Arp was included (German Wikipedia, relayed by the Kunstmuseum Basel retrospective page)
stops.campa: The first documenta opens in the Museum Fridericianum on the sixteenth of July, in a building bombed out and patched up for the purpose, and runs to September. Its business is to put back in front of Germans the modern art the Reich had taken down, sold and burned. Sophie Taeuber-Arp is in it, twelve years dead. This is not a rediscovery. The organizers are of her own generation and knew the work when it was new. The cataloguing of it under her husband's name goes on regardless.
suggested_refs: documenta 1, Museum Fridericianum, Kassel, 16 July to 18 September 1955

stops.name: New York, 11 West 53rd Street
stops.date_confidence: The address is attested (English Wikipedia, 'Museum of Modern Art'), and the dossier's note that the 1936 show sat at a prior address is wrong: MoMA has occupied 11 West 53rd Street since 1932, the 1939 building going up on the same site. Her inclusion in the December 1936 exhibition 'Fantastic Art, Dada, Surrealism' is dossier-only and remains [R], moma.org having returned 403 on every route attempted. The 1981 retrospective is attested by German Wikipedia's exhibition list; its tour to Chicago, Houston and Montreal, and the claim that it was MoMA's first for her, are [R]. The stop is dated to the 1981 retrospective, the attested event of the two, which also keeps it in sequence within this segment; the 1936 appearance is narrated inside it. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Her work reaches Fifty-Third Street twice, forty-five years apart. In 1936 a few pieces go into a survey of fantastic art, Dada and surrealism, among hundreds of others, if the chronologies are right; the museum's own records could not be opened to check. In 1981 the museum gives her a retrospective of her own, catalogued by Carolyn Lanchner. It is the first American institution to hang her as a body of work and not as a name under a group photograph. Whether it travelled on to Chicago, Houston and Montreal is unconfirmed.
suggested_refs: Carolyn Lanchner, 'Sophie Taeuber-Arp', Museum of Modern Art, New York, 1981, exhibition catalogue
sources: moma.org: inaccessible, HTTP 403 on all routes attempted

stops.name: Bern, the fifty-franc note
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Swiss National Bank's eighth-series 50-franc note carrying her portrait was issued 3 October 1995 and ceased to be legal tender 30 April 2021, with four of her works on the reverse, Relief rectangulaire (1936), Tete Dada (1919), Composition Aubette (1927) and Lignes ouvertes (1939) (Swiss National Bank, banknote series page). English Wikipedia gives a different active-circulation window, 1995 to 2016; the SNB is the primary source and the discrepancy is left standing. The April 2025 Christie's sale mentioned in the campa is attested at about EUR 3.06 million on 8 April 2025
stops.campa: The national bank puts her face on the fifty-franc note, the only woman given as principal subject anywhere in the eighth series, and prints four of her works on the back: a relief from 1936, a Dada head from 1919, an Aubette composition from 1927, a sheet of open lines from 1939. For a quarter of a century the country that let her teach embroidery and then let her leave carries her in its pockets. In April 2025 one of those reliefs sells at Christie's in Paris for about three million euros. She was never paid anything remotely like it.
suggested_refs: Swiss National Bank eighth banknote series, 50-franc note, 1995-2021
Christie's Paris, 8 April 2025, Relief rond en quatre hauteurs
sources: heni.com news report of the April 2025 Christie's sale

stops.name: Kunstmuseum Basel, Living Abstraction
stops.date_confidence: attested: 'Sophie Taeuber-Arp: Living Abstraction' ran at the Kunstmuseum Basel 20 March to 20 June 2021, then Tate Modern 15 July to 17 October 2021, billed there as the first retrospective of her work ever held in the United Kingdom, then MoMA 21 November 2021 to 12 March 2022 (Kunstmuseum Basel exhibition page and Tate exhibition page, both fetched). MoMA's own dates could not be reconfirmed directly, moma.org returning 403. The correspondence edition is corrected against Hyperallergic: the Nimbus set is 'Sophie Taeuber-Arp: Briefe 1905-1942' (2021), and the Mueller-Widmann volume holds 35 letters written between 1932 and 1942, most of them predating the war
stops.campa: Three museums mount one exhibition and call it Living Abstraction: Basel, then London, then New York. Britain, which had never given her a retrospective, gives her one seventy-eight years after her death. In the same seasons a German edition of her correspondence appears, drawn from some four hundred and fifty unpublished letters and postcards that the Zentralbibliothek Zuerich bought in 2012, with an annotated English edition of the letters to the Mueller-Widmanns behind it. For the first time the sources on her are mostly her own sentences.
stops.quote: Only when we go into ourselves and attempt to be entirely true to ourselves will we succeed in making things of value, living things, and in this way help to develop a new style that is fitting for us.
stops.quote_source: Sophie Taeuber-Arp, quoted by Tate, 'Five things to know about Sophie Taeuber-Arp'; no primary text is named for it by any source reached
suggested_refs: Sophie Taeuber-Arp: Briefe 1905-1942, Nimbus, 2021, edited by Medea Hoch, Walburga Krupp and Sigrid Schade
The Mueller-Widmann letters, Fondazione Marguerite Arp and Scheidegger & Spiess, 2022
sources: Tate, 'Five things to know about Sophie Taeuber-Arp'
Hyperallergic, 'The Patrons Who Sustained Sophie Taeuber-Arp'
